Toxicology Chapter 204

Industrial Toxins

Industrial toxicology is a pattern-and-time-course chapter. The board traps are poor warning properties, delayed pulmonary edema, skin absorption, severe lactic acidosis from cyanide, and rapid collapse from hydrogen sulfide.

Board lens: stabilize and decontaminate first, but do not wait for confirmatory cyanide levels when the clinical pattern is severe. Antidotes are time-sensitive.

Triage and Monitoring

Industrial toxin cases start as scene-safety and physiology problems, not as memorization of a chemical name. The ED priorities are to protect staff, remove the patient from ongoing exposure, decontaminate when needed, stabilize airway/breathing/circulation, and then decide who needs prolonged observation.

First move: PPE and source control come before bedside heroics. Remove contaminated clothing, bag belongings, irrigate exposed skin/eyes when appropriate, and keep staff out of the contamination path.

Dermal Absorption Is Not Benign

Some industrial chemicals cross intact skin and can produce systemic toxicity even when the patient looks only mildly contaminated. Clothing and skin can keep delivering toxin after arrival, so decontamination is part of resuscitation rather than housekeeping.

Tintinalli source check

Table 204-1 - agents absorbed through intact skin

Use this table early when exposure involves liquid, solvent, pesticide, nitrile, phenol, hydrofluoric acid, or unknown industrial splash.

Initial ED bundle

Remove from source, PPE, clothing removal, skin/eye irrigation, high-flow oxygen if symptomatic, ECG, pulse oximetry, ABG/VBG when ill, lactate, COHb, and MetHb when the syndrome fits.

Consult early

Poison center, medical toxicology, HazMat/EMS report, occupational health, and the workplace safety data sheet can change antidote choice and prevent secondary exposure.

Delayed Toxicity Is the Board Trap

A patient may arrive with normal vital signs after a dangerous exposure. The disposition question is not “do they look fine now?” but “does this toxin have a delayed pulmonary, metabolic, hematologic, or neurologic phase?”

Tintinalli source check

Table 204-2 - delayed onset or prolonged monitoring

Keep these agents in observation even when early symptoms are limited; several declare toxicity hours later.

Disposition anchor: phosgene, methyl bromide, methylene chloride, nitriles, aniline, arsine, and phosphine should push you toward observation or admission based on symptoms, concentration, enclosed-space exposure, and comorbidity.
Rosen source check

Rosen Table 148.1 - inhaled toxins as bedside classes

Rosen Ch.148 organizes inhaled industrial toxins by source and physiologic class: simple asphyxiant, chemical asphyxiant, irritant by solubility, free-radical injury, or mixed smoke exposure.

Tintinalli spine

Tintinalli Ch.204 lists which industrial agents require decontamination, delayed monitoring, respiratory observation, and cyanide treatment.

Rosen vs Tintinalli

Rosen adds a class map that links source/use to the dominant physiologic failure, including hydrogen cyanide, hydrogen sulfide, chlorine, phosgene, ammonia, sulfur dioxide, and smoke.

ED / exam decision

Use the class to plan monitoring: simple asphyxiants improve after removal/oxygen, highly soluble irritants declare early, poorly soluble irritants need longer observation, and chemical asphyxiants require acid-base/lactate thinking.

Respiratory Industrial Toxins

Respiratory industrial toxins are organized by warning properties, water solubility, and time course. Upper-airway irritation can be immediate and dramatic, while distal alveolar injury can be deceptively delayed.

Tintinalli source check

Table 204-3 - respiratory symptoms and treatment

This table belongs beside the respiratory discussion because the board asks you to connect the agent to onset, observation, and supportive care.

Phosgene

Phosgene has poor warning properties. Early eye/nose/throat irritation may be mild or absent, but lower-airway injury can progress to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema over the next 24 hours. The classic odor is freshly cut hay, but odor is not a safety tool.

  • Mandatory rest: exertion can worsen pulmonary edema.
  • Observe even minimally symptomatic patients after meaningful exposure.
  • Treat with oxygen if hypoxemic, bronchodilators for bronchospasm, and lung-protective ventilatory support if respiratory failure develops.

Chlorine

Chlorine has excellent warning properties: pungent odor, eye and upper-airway burning, cough, nausea/vomiting, and bronchospasm. Severe exposure can still produce pulmonary edema, usually within hours.

  • Care is primarily supportive: humidified oxygen, bronchodilators, and eye/skin irrigation when contaminated.
  • Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended.
  • Nebulized sodium bicarbonate may be considered for selected symptomatic chlorine/hydrogen chloride exposures, but it is not a substitute for airway assessment.

Nitrogen Dioxide and Ammonia

Nitrogen dioxide can cause a triphasic illness: mild initial symptoms, transient improvement, then delayed pulmonary edema 24 to 72 hours later. Ammonia is highly water-soluble and alkali, causing immediate mucosal and ocular irritation with risk of lower-airway injury after high concentration exposure.

Board distinction: immediate irritation does not always mean mild disease, and minimal early irritation does not always mean safe discharge. Time course plus solubility decides observation.
Rosen source check

Rosen Figure 148.1 - irritant gases reacting with airway water

Rosen gives the chemical mechanism behind acid, alkali, and oxidant airway injury. This explains why solubility predicts where and when symptoms appear.

Tintinalli spine

Tintinalli emphasizes warning properties and timing: chlorine declares early, while phosgene may progress after a quiet initial exam.

Rosen vs Tintinalli

Rosen makes the solubility mechanism explicit. Highly water-soluble gases injure eyes and upper airway early; poorly water-soluble gases can reach distal alveoli and cause delayed edema.

ED / exam decision

Do not discharge a patient after phosgene or heavy closed-space exposure simply because the first exam is quiet. Use serial lung exam, pulse oximetry, CXR when symptomatic, and observation.

Cyanide

Cyanide causes histotoxic hypoxia: oxygen may be present in the blood, but cells cannot use it effectively. The clinical problem is rapid failure of high-demand organs, especially brain and heart.

Sources and Exposure Patterns

Think cyanide after industrial exposure, laboratory/metal work, fumigants, nitriles, and especially smoke inhalation from nitrogen-containing materials. The source history is helpful, but the unstable patient should not wait for a confirmed chemical inventory.

Tintinalli source check

Table 204-4 - sources of cyanide

Use this table to connect the exposure setting to cyanide risk, especially fires, plastics, electroplating, fumigants, and nitrile-related exposures.

Pathophysiology

Cyanide binds cytochrome oxidase in the mitochondrial electron transport chain. ATP production fails, anaerobic metabolism rises, and lactate accumulates. Pulse oximetry can look reassuring because hemoglobin oxygen carriage is not the primary defect.

Rosen source check

Rosen Figure 148.2 - cyanide and hydrogen sulfide block Complex IV

Rosen links cyanide, hydrogen sulfide, and carbon monoxide to failure of oxidative phosphorylation, lactate generation, and cellular hypoxia despite apparently adequate oxygenation.

Tintinalli spine

Tintinalli frames severe cyanide as altered mental status, shock, seizures/coma, cardiovascular collapse, and severe lactic acidosis; smoke inhalation with lactate >10 mmol/L is a key clue.

Rosen vs Tintinalli

Rosen states lactate >8 mmol/L is highly predictive in the right context and emphasizes that pulse oximetry and ABG oxygenation may appear acceptable in isolated cyanide or H2S poisoning.

ED / exam decision

Treat the patient, not the cyanide level. Fire or industrial exposure plus coma, shock, seizure, bradycardia/dysrhythmia, or severe lactate should trigger antidote planning immediately.

Clinical Features

Severe poisoning is abrupt and dramatic: headache or anxiety can progress to hyperventilation, altered mental status, seizures, hypotension, bradycardia, cardiovascular collapse, coma, and death. Cyanosis is not required early and bitter-almond odor is unreliable.

Tintinalli source check

Table 204-5 - acute cyanide toxicity

This table is a severity ladder: CNS and cardiovascular deterioration are more important than odor or a send-out cyanide level.

Diagnostic Pattern

Do not wait for whole-blood cyanide results. The ED pattern is exposure risk plus high anion gap metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, shock, coma/seizure, or unexpectedly severe illness. In smoke inhalation, consider concomitant carbon monoxide and cyanide together.

Board trap: normal SpO2 or normal PaO2 does not rule out cyanide; the danger signal is exposure plus shock, coma/seizure, and severe lactate/acidosis.
Tintinalli source check

Table 204-6 - anticipated laboratory findings

Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude cyanide. Lactate and acid-base status carry more bedside weight.

Treatment: Hydroxocobalamin First When Smoke/CO Is Possible

Give 100% oxygen, support ventilation and circulation, treat seizures, and do not delay antidote therapy in severe suspected poisoning. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin and is favored when smoke inhalation or carbon monoxide coexposure is possible because it does not intentionally create methemoglobin.

Tintinalli source check

Table 204-7 - hydroxocobalamin treatment

This table belongs in the cyanide treatment section because the dose is part of the immediate antidote decision.

Treatment: Cyanide Antidote Kit and Nitrite Caution

The classic cyanide antidote kit uses nitrites to induce methemoglobin and sodium thiosulfate to enhance conversion to thiocyanate. This is not benign in smoke inhalation: nitrites can worsen oxygen delivery when COHb is elevated or severe hypotension is present.

Tintinalli source check

Table 204-8 - cyanide antidote kit dosing

Keep this source image with cyanide treatment, not in the generic dose appendix, because it contains the key nitrite warning.

Rosen source check

Rosen Box 148.2 - cyanide antidotes and the nitrite trap

Rosen separates hydroxocobalamin from the classic two-part cyanide antidote kit and explicitly flags when nitrites should be withheld.

Tintinalli spine

Tintinalli gives hydroxocobalamin and classic cyanide antidote kit dosing in Tables 204-7 and 204-8.

Rosen vs Tintinalli

Rosen sharpens the smoke-inhalation decision: nitrites create methemoglobin and can worsen oxygen delivery, so withhold nitrites when elevated COHb is suspected.

ED / exam decision

For the unstable smoke-inhalation patient with suspected cyanide, hydroxocobalamin is the board-favored early antidote because it does not intentionally reduce oxygen-carrying capacity.

Disposition

Admit symptomatic patients, anyone receiving antidotal therapy, and patients with smoke inhalation plus concerning lactate, neurologic findings, cardiovascular instability, or delayed-risk ingestion such as nitriles. Recovery can occur if treatment is rapid, but delayed neuropsychiatric injury is possible after severe hypoxic events.

Hydrogen Sulfide

Hydrogen sulfide is both a pulmonary irritant and a chemical asphyxiant. It is encountered in sewers, manure pits, petroleum work, mines, asphalt, and industrial or chemical-suicide scenes. The first patient may be a rescuer.

Scene safety: the rotten-egg odor is not protective. High concentrations cause olfactory fatigue/paralysis, so absence of odor does not mean absence of danger.

Pathophysiology and Presentation

Like cyanide, hydrogen sulfide inhibits mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Massive exposure can cause sudden collapse after a few breaths, seizures, coma, dysrhythmias, and death. Survivors may have ocular injury, bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, and delayed neurologic injury.

  • Low-level exposure: eye/throat irritation, cough, nausea, headache.
  • High-level exposure: rapid loss of consciousness, apnea, shock, seizures, and cardiovascular collapse.
  • Delayed issues: corneal injury, pulmonary edema, and neuropsychiatric sequelae after severe hypoxia.

ED Management

Remove from exposure only with trained rescue and appropriate respiratory protection. In the ED, give high-flow oxygen, decontaminate skin and eyes, support ventilation and circulation, treat seizures, and monitor for delayed pulmonary complications.

Sodium nitrite may be considered in severe early presentations with altered sensorium or cardiovascular dysfunction, especially if given within minutes, but supportive care and safe rescue are the core treatment.

Rosen source check

Rosen Ch.148 - hydrogen sulfide rescue risk and olfactory fatigue

Rosen discusses hydrogen sulfide with cyanide-like chemical asphyxiants. The key additions are responder safety, chemical-suicide/industrial scene risk, olfactory fatigue, and rapid mitochondrial dissociation in some survivors.

Tintinalli spine

Tintinalli focuses on sewers, manure pits, petroleum settings, rotten-egg odor unreliability, sudden collapse, pulmonary edema, corneal injury, and early nitrite consideration for severe cases.

Rosen vs Tintinalli

Rosen reinforces that odor cannot protect rescuers and that H2S shares cyanide-like Complex IV toxicity, but may dissociate rapidly after brief exposure.

ED / exam decision

Do not let staff enter a contaminated zone. Remove with trained rescue, give oxygen and ventilatory support, decontaminate skin/eyes, and consider nitrite only in the early severe window.

Drug Dose Reference

This section is a quick dose recap. The full source treatment tables are embedded in the cyanide section where the clinical decision is made.

TherapyDose / UseBoard Notes
HydroxocobalaminAdult 5 g IV over 15 min; may repeat once. Pediatric 70 mg/kg IV, max 5 g.Preferred when smoke inhalation or possible CO coexposure makes nitrites risky. Can discolor skin/urine and interfere with some labs.
100% oxygenImmediate supportive therapy for cyanide, H2S, CO/smoke, and symptomatic inhaled irritants.Do not wait for confirmatory cyanide levels in severe suspected poisoning.
Sodium thiosulfateAdult 12.5 g IV in cyanide kit; repeat half-dose if symptoms persist.Low toxicity sulfur donor; often paired with nitrite in the classic kit.
Sodium nitriteAdult 300 mg IV over at least 5 min for cyanide kit; for severe early H2S, 300 mg IV over 2-4 min may be considered.Creates methemoglobin. Avoid/caution with smoke inhalation, COHb elevation, severe hypotension, or unclear diagnosis.
Bronchodilators / humidified oxygenSupportive care for irritant gas bronchospasm.Routine prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended after chlorine/phosgene exposure.
